content.title: About
content.content: Pumpkin seeds are the edible kernels of pumpkin (Cucurbita pepo) that are traditionally enjoyed as a salted snack. They have a mild nutty flavor with a pronounced salty note and a crunchy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pumpkin seeds are rich in magnesium, iron, and zinc.
Ancient cultures used them as a portable source of energy for travel and hunting.
They are one of the few plant sources of heart‑healthy triglycerides.
In the United States more than 1 billion pounds of pumpkin seeds are produced each year.
Salted seeds are a popular bar snack and often served with beer.

items.title: Rich in magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle, nerve, and cardiovascular function.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc is essential for immune health and wound healing.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Pumpkin seeds provide vitamin E and carotenoids that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports prostate health
items.content: Research suggests that zinc and phytosterols in the seeds may benefit prostate function.

items.title: Provides plant protein
items.content: One cup of seeds delivers about 30 g of protein, making them a valuable source for vegetarians.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pumpkin seeds.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Salted varieties can contribute to elevated blood pressure if consumed in excess.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Seeds are calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Additives
items.content: Commercial products may contain artificial flavorings and preservatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Seeds can be eaten straight as a snack, added to salads, yogurt, granola, baked goods, or used as a topping for soups. They are often roasted and salted before consumption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent the fats from becoming rancid.
